title: Como Robotics resignation cluster: 'hot market churn' versus post-complaint retaliation risk
scenario_text:
Como Robotics sees five resignations in eight weeks from one 22-person hardware team. In the #people-ops Slack channel the HR business partner writes: 'This is the hot robotics talent market - everyone's poaching senior mechanical engineers right now. It's voluntary churn, comp-driven. I'd recommend a market pay adjustment for the team to stem it. Nothing unusual here.' Posted Monday.

Other systems raise a different pattern. In the HRIS, all five departures report to the same engineering manager, hired six months ago; no other team under that director shows elevated attrition. In the ethics-hotline case system, an anonymous complaint alleging that manager falsified safety-test sign-offs was filed nine weeks ago - one week before the first resignation. In the exit-interview records, three of the five cite 'concerns about how issues get raised' and 'retaliation' in free-text, though the coded reason is 'compensation.' In the access-log system, two departing employees had recently downloaded internal safety-test datasets. And in email, a retained team member wrote to the HRBP last week: 'People are leaving because they flagged the test problem and got sidelined.'

Each signal is individually explainable: senior engineers are in demand, one manager can have bad luck, exit free-text is venting, and data downloads happen before departures. But together - departures concentrated under one newly hired manager, a safety-falsification complaint filed just before the exodus began, exit text naming retaliation despite a 'compensation' code, and a retained employee corroborating - they describe possible retaliation tied to a protected safety complaint, not a market-comp problem. The HRBP's 'hot market' read predates reading the exit free-text and the hotline timeline. You lead People Ops. What should you do?
question: What should the People Ops lead do about the resignation cluster?
choices: Approve a market pay adjustment for the team to stem comp-driven attrition, as the HRBP recommended.
Run stay interviews and a broader engagement survey for the team before taking any other action.

Open a formal investigation with employment counsel into the manager and possible retaliation, and preserve the safety complaint and related records: the timing after the safety complaint, the single-manager concentration, exit text naming retaliation, and corroboration point to a protected-activity issue, not market churn.
Coach the new manager on retention best practices and monitor attrition for another quarter.
